animal sacrifices
------------------------------------------
Sacrificing an animal to please a supernatural deity is a common feature found in many cultures, including that of हिन्दुइस्म्, during the early part of their development. Though formal animal sacri-fices of the early Vedic period gradually lost their importance, due to the reformatory movements of the Upaniṣadic sages, जैनिस्म् and बुद्धिस्म्, a new type of animal sacrifice got into the fabric of हिन्दुइस्म् during later ages, as aboriginal cultures got integrated into the Hindu fold.
The deity was invariably an aspect of दुर्गा or Kālī and the rituals were very simple. Buffaloes, goats, sheep and cockerels were the usual sacrificial victims. It was believed that these victims would go to हेअवेन्.
Various reform movements have helped to minimise this practice.
See also NIRŪḌHA PAŚUBANDHA and SOMAYĀGA.

Aniruddha
(‘unobstructed’)
------------------------------------------
Aniruddha was the son of प्रद्युम्न and grandson of कृष्ण. Uṣā, the daughter of Bāṇāsura, fell in love with him and got him magically transported to her palace. Though Bāṇāsura discovered it and tried his best to destroy him, he did not succeed. Ultimately अनिरुद्ध and Uṣā were married.
The भागवत or the Pāñcarātra cult (a form of वैष्णविस्म्) considers अनिरुद्ध as one of the four व्यूहस् or emanations of Lord विष्णु. (See CATURVYŪHAS.) Symbolically, he represents the चोस्मिच् मिन्द्.
See also PĀÑCARĀTRA ĀGAMA.

anitya
(‘non-eternal’)
------------------------------------------
Time, space and causation are great destroyers. Everything in this created world comes under their sway and hence gets changed, modified, decayed and des-troyed. All such objects are called अनित्य as opposed to नित्य which is the eternal unchanging principle. Hindu philosophical systems generally accept the आत्मन् and God as नित्य and other things like the external objects or the body as अनित्य.
See also NITYA.
